progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: C01 (follow the proton; Brønsted-Lowry acid and base; HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻; NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻; water can be the acid or the base; HCO₃⁻ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ + OH⁻ met in C01 attempt 1; H₃O⁺ is hydronium). C02 (polyatomic ion names, including hydrogen carbonate, carbonate, phosphate, dihydrogen phosphate, hydrogen phosphate; carbonic acid breaks down into water and carbon dioxide). C05 (strong acid ionises completely, single arrow; weak acid partly, double arrow; acetate takes protons back; dynamic equilibrium). Year 11: ionic salts dissolve into ions; balancing charge. Not assumed: Kw, pH calculation, Ka.
progression.startsWith: Follow one proton-transfer equation. The video opens: Sprinkle baking soda into hydrochloric acid, and it fizzes, and the solution becomes less acidic. Now sprinkle it into sodium hydroxide solution. No fizz this time, but the solution becomes less basic.
progression.stopsAfter: identifying the Brønsted-Lowry acid and base and both conjugate pairs in a given equation, with one proton and one charge between partners; writing a conjugate acid or base for a given species; explaining with conjugate strength why a strong acid gets → and a weak acid ⇌; explaining why a species is amphiprotic and spotting one from a proton chain; writing the dissolving equation and both water equations for sodium hydrogen carbonate or potassium dihydrogen phosphate; writing water's self-ionisation and saying what neutral means. No Kw value, pH or temperature effects (chem-m6-c07), no Ka or Kb (chem-m6-c10), no salt hydrolysis predictions, no buffers (chem-m6-c11).
progression.nextLesson: putting a number on water's self-ionisation and calculating pH for strong acids and bases (route chem-m6-c07).

teaching.task: Baking soda calms an acid, and it also calms a base. How can one ion act as a base in one reaction and an acid in another, and what are the "conjugate" partners that every acid-base reaction makes?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) one powder calms an acid and a base: how can one substance play both roles? (1); (2) run a known proton transfer backwards: the products are also an acid and a base, so every reaction can swap the proton back (2); (3) conjugate base and conjugate acid: linked by exactly one proton, charge changes by one, opposite sides (3); (4) worked example: follow the proton in HPO₄²⁻ + H₂O; one proton per pair, so H₂SO₄ pairs with HSO₄⁻ (4); (5) a strong acid's conjugate base has almost no pull on a proton, so the reaction goes all the way (→); a weak acid's conjugate base pulls protons back (⇌) (5); (6) hydrogen carbonate takes a proton from hydronium (fizz) and gives one to hydroxide (no gas): amphiprotic (6); (7) in a proton chain the middle species can give and take; the ends do one job (7); (8) a salt dissolves into a spectator ion and the amphiprotic ion; one water equation for each role (8); (9) water is the middle of its own chain, so it reacts with itself; a tiny equilibrium in equal amounts; neutral means equal (9); memory aid (10); two attempts and brief feedback (11 to 14); decision rule and handoff (15); key notes (16).
teaching.conversationalApproach: one powder, baking soda, calms both an acid and a base. Running a known proton transfer backwards shows that the products are also an acid and a base, which gives conjugate pairs; conjugate strength explains the single and double arrows; hydrogen carbonate is then shown taking a proton in one reaction and giving one in another, as the middle of a proton chain, and water turns out to be the middle of its own chain. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Sprinkle baking soda into hydrochloric acid, and it fizzes, and the solution becomes less acidic. Now sprinkle it into sodium hydroxide solution. No fizz this time, but the solution becomes less basic. The same white powder calms an acid and calms a base. So how can one substance act as a base in one reaction, and as an acid in another?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "Potassium dihydrogen phosphate, KH₂PO₄, is used in foods as an acidity regulator. Write an equation for KH₂PO₄ dissolving in water. Then write two equations, each with water as the reaction partner, to show that the dihydrogen phosphate ion is amphiprotic." The second syllabus salt (the video works sodium hydrogen carbonate); the chain in scene 7 names the species but writes none of these equations. Crossed mistake: "H₂PO₄⁻ + H₂O ⇌ PO₄³⁻ + ..." (two protons in one step). (A2) "NH₄⁺(aq) + CO₃²⁻(aq) ⇌ NH₃(aq) + HCO₃⁻(aq). Identify the two conjugate acid-base pairs in this reaction, and state which species is the Brønsted-Lowry acid." New equation with no water in it. Crossed mistake: "NH₄⁺ / CO₃²⁻ is a pair" (same side).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "write ionic equations to represent the dissociation of acids and bases in water, conjugate acid/base pairs in solution and amphiprotic nature of some salts, for example:; sodium hydrogen carbonate; potassium dihydrogen phosphate" this video starts from one proton-transfer equation the student already knows (NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻, C01) and runs it backwards to find the conjugate pairs. It teaches: conjugate acid and base and the one-proton, one-charge rule; identifying both pairs in an unfamiliar equation (the site's HPO₄²⁻ example); conjugate strength, used to explain C05's arrows; amphiprotic species, with sodium hydrogen carbonate reacting both ways (the hook), the proton chain for spotting them (carbonate, phosphate, water), and the dissolving equation plus both water equations for a syllabus salt; water's self-ionisation as water's own role, with "neutral means equal hydronium and hydroxide". It stops at identifying pairs, water's role and an amphiprotic species. Not here: Kw as a number, pH and pOH, and neutral pH at other temperatures (chem-m6-c07, whose route start assumes complete ionisation and whose pOH method needs Kw; scene 15 hands off to it); Ka, Kb and Ka × Kb = Kw (chem-m6-c10); predicting which way an amphiprotic ion reacts from Ka values (the site's HPO₄²⁻ "Kb > Ka3" example; chem-m6-c10 and buffers chem-m6-c11); salt hydrolysis (see Open decisions); buffers (chem-m6-c11); "amphoteric" (author note e). The Kohlrausch history is not used (register draft correction).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key on screen throughout (C01): the proton is a small teal token; a donor (acid) gets an amber outline; an acceptor (base) a violet outline; water pale blue; pair brackets in matching colours (amber pair above the equation, violet pair below); spent labels grey. Board layout (constant): the short question top-left in one line; the equation strip centre; pair brackets above and below it; a plate or lens at the right only when it carries the explanation. Clutter rule: at most three bright text items at once; every tag dims when its sentence ends. Reuse: painted plates (inspected 19 Oct): `m6-baking-soda-box-v1.png` (hook and scene 8), `m6-clip-baking-soda-vinegar-before-v1.png` (white powder resting in clear liquid, no bubbles) and `m6-clip-baking-soda-vinegar-fizz-v1.png` (the same beaker fizzing; aligned pair). In the hook the left beaker uses the pair with the coded label "hydrochloric acid" (the plates show only a clear liquid; nothing in them reads as vinegar), and the right beaker uses the "before" plate alone with the coded label "sodium hydroxide solution", so it stays quiet. `m5x-ammonia-bottle-v1.png` (scene 2, small). `m6-beaker-v1.png` (scene 9, "very pure water"). Not used: `m6-ph-meter-probe-beaker-v1.png` (no pH numbers before c07; the hook shows the change as a coded arrow toward neutral). No new plates needed. No human figures.
design.transitionPlan: The baking soda plate and the two clip plates open the puzzle; the equation strip runs forward and then backwards with the teal token hopping; pair brackets draw above and below the strip in matching colours; the proton chain builds as a row of species; the salt equations stack one per role; water self-ionisation writes as its own chain; the memory aid writes large; each attempt clears the board and its feedback underlines the question; the decision rule card and next chip close; scene crossfade with settle.
